scenario: The athlete uploads three years of Garmin exports mid-conversation, then asks 我這一年跑量的變化怎麼樣？上週呢？
given: The upload landed as reported activities carrying source athlete_imported and imported_from naming the athlete's own label for the file.
Last week holds two prescribed runs; the provider has an activity attached to each, and the upload also holds a session on one of those two days at the same sport.
That overlapping row carries provider_actual_same_day true; the other imported rows for the week carry it false.
The upload's rows carry no activity id, no match confidence and no completion, and none appears in recent_actuals.
Nothing in the upload is newer than the day the Intervals connection was made except that one overlapping row.

expected.conclusion: The uploaded years are usable history and the coach says what they show, while last week's account of planned versus actual still rests on the provider's activities; the one overlapping day is named as one session, not two.
must_state: That the long-range trend is read from the athlete's own upload, naming it as such rather than as measured history this product observed.
Last week's planned-versus-actual from the provider's attached activities, unchanged by the upload.
That the overlapping day is one session the upload and the provider both describe, so it counts once.
Which of the two questions the evidence can actually answer, and which it cannot.
must_not_state: That an uploaded session completed a planned session, or any claim that the upload changed what was delivered or reconciled.
A weekly volume for last week that counts the overlapping session twice, once as the upload's and once as the provider's.
That the imported years are provider data, an Intervals record, or something this product measured.
A trend figure, percentage, or fitness verdict computed from the upload as though it were a measurement.

fails_if: The answer folds imported rows into the week's actuals, which is the double count the whole ingress boundary exists to prevent: one week of training read as two the moment an athlete uploads a file covering it.
The answer refuses to use the uploaded years at all because they are not provider-backed, which throws away the only record of everything before the connection existed.
The answer treats provider_actual_same_day as a merge instruction and silently drops one of the two rows instead of reading them as one session described twice.
